open-question.question: In what form does the rendered Antigravity tree name the global plugin root in every path it reads and every python3 command it runs — a tilde path (~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn), a $HOME-prefixed path, the ${PLUGIN_ROOT} string the agy binary carries for MCP and hook configuration, or a prose rule telling the runner to resolve the root from the absolute SKILL.md path the host loads a skill from — given that the one literal must resolve both in the host's file-reading tool and in a shell command, in the orchestrator and in a dispatched agent whose prompt carries no plugin path?
open-question.alternative: The literal is fixed when the tree is built. plugin_root in scripts/hosts/antigravity/settings.toml becomes "~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn", so every one of the 96 sites in the rendered tree reads like `python3 ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn/tools/open_questions.py …` or `~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn/shared/….md`. The same text goes to the orchestrator and to both agents. The dispatch prompts and core/ stay as they are, and the runner gets no resolution rule. It is the smallest change: one settings value. It is the conventional way to write a home path, the shell expands it in every rendered command (the path always starts a word, including inside the batch call's `"$(…)"` substitution), and it is the exact form the host's own plugin guide uses. So the orchestrator and an agent whose prompt holds no plugin path see the same self-contained path. The host's file-reading tool is not a shell. Nobody has checked whether it expands `~`, so file reads of shared procedures work only if the runner turns `~` into an absolute path itself, and the report's failures were partly on exactly those reads. The shell also leaves a tilde unexpanded inside quotes or in the middle of a word, so any later edit that quotes a path breaks it without an error.

The literal is fixed when the tree is built. plugin_root becomes "$HOME/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn", so every rendered command reads `python3 $HOME/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn/tools/….py …` and every read path reads `$HOME/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn/shared/….md`. Orchestrator and agents see the same text. The dispatch prompts and core/ stay as they are, and the runner gets no resolution rule. Like the tilde, this is a one-value change that needs no prompt change. Unlike the tilde, the shell expands it inside double quotes and in the middle of a word as well as at the start, so a command stays correct even if a later edit quotes or concatenates the path. The environment provides $HOME rather than the runner defining it, so the rule against shell variables does not cover it. The file-reading tool does no more environment-variable expansion than a tilde gets, so reads again depend on the runner substituting the home directory. A `$HOME` read path also looks less like a path than `~` does, which makes it more likely that a model passes the string through unchanged. Inside single quotes it does not expand at all.

Substitution is left to the host at run time. plugin_root becomes "${PLUGIN_ROOT}", the string the agy binary carries for MCP and hook configuration. The tree relies on the host replacing that string with the plugin's absolute directory in skill and agent text before the runner sees it, the way the Codex tree already relies on the same literal. Dispatch prompts and core/ stay as they are, and the runner gets no rule. If the host does substitute it, both surfaces get a real absolute path, in the orchestrator and in a dispatched agent alike, with no dependence on how the runner expands paths. It would work for any install location, not just the global one. The foreign-plugin-root check already exempts two hosts that share one literal, so the build needs no change. The host's built-in guides document no substitution into skill or agent text, and nobody has checked whether it happens. If it does not, a command's `${PLUGIN_ROOT}` expands to an empty string in the shell (giving `/tools/open_questions.py`), and a read gets the literal string. That reproduces the reported failure everywhere, and the goal's global-path standardization would then appear nowhere in the tree.

The runner resolves the root at run time. plugin_root becomes a fixed token that stands for "the plugin root". A prose rule in the runtime files tells the orchestrator to take the absolute SKILL.md path the host shows in its skill metadata and remove `skills/<skill>/SKILL.md` to get the root, then write that absolute path into every read and command. Dispatched agents get no such metadata, and the host hands an agent its file's instructions without the agent reading the file, so the orchestrator also passes the resolved root as an extra value in each dispatch prompt: the alternatives prompt and the complete-all-tasks prompt each get a fourth or second value, and the agent files list it as an input. Every read and every command gets a real absolute path taken from where the host actually loaded the plugin, so file reads do not depend on tilde or variable expansion, and the tree is correct wherever the plugin is installed. The dispatch-prompt rule allows the extra value, because the orchestrator holds it and the agent cannot fetch it. It is the largest change. A resolution rule and a new prompt value have to reach core/ in a form that names no host and means something in every tree, so either a new slot or a prompt change that the Claude Code and Codex trees do not need. Every one of the 96 sites then depends on the runner applying a prose rule correctly instead of copying a literal, and a runner that skips the rule is back to the reported failure.

The literal is resolved when the plugin is installed. plugin_root becomes a fixed sentinel string with no `{{`, and the README's Antigravity install command, after extracting into ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn, rewrites that sentinel in the extracted files to the user's absolute home path. The installed tree then reads `python3 /Users/<user>/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn/tools/….py` and `/Users/<user>/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn/shared/….md` everywhere. Dispatch prompts and core/ stay as they are, and the runner gets no rule. It is the only option that puts a plain absolute path in every read and every command, for orchestrator and agents alike, with no tilde or variable expansion, no unverified host substitution, and no prose rule left for the runner to apply. The published tree is no longer what gets installed. Until the rewrite runs, the tree carries a sentinel that makes no sense as a path, the install becomes a multi-step shell pipeline whose in-place rewrite behaves differently on BSD and GNU, and a home directory that moves means reinstalling. Any check that compares the installed copy with hosts/antigravity/ byte for byte stops holding, so it depends on which plugin copy the agy suite drives.

open-question.question: How does the enable_write_tools: true frontmatter key reach the two rendered Antigravity agent files — written into core/agents/*.md and stripped from the Claude Code and Codex trees through their strip_frontmatter_keys as color is today, added at render time by a new per-host build setting that inserts frontmatter keys, or written into the core files and left standing in every host's tree as a key the other hosts ignore?
open-question.alternative: Write `enable_write_tools: true` into the frontmatter of both `core/agents/*.md` files beside `color`. Claude Code's `strip_frontmatter_keys` goes from `[]` to `["enable_write_tools"]`, Codex's from `["color"]` to `["color", "enable_write_tools"]`, and Antigravity's stays `["color"]`, so the key survives only in `hosts/antigravity/agents/`. No build code changes. The existing `stripped-key-present` check already fails a Claude Code or Codex tree that still carries the key. It reuses the one frontmatter mechanism the build already has and tests, the same path `color` takes today, so the change is two core lines and two settings lists. A tree that leaks the key is caught by an existing check at build and `--check` time. `core/` would carry a second host-specific mechanism key, and the invariant that calls `color` "the one structural exception" would have to be widened. The model also becomes subtractive: any future host inherits the write-and-shell grant unless its definition remembers to strip it, and Claude Code's strip list, empty until now, starts naming another host's key.

Leave `core/agents/*.md` unchanged and add a new required setting to `SETTINGS_SCHEMA` in `scripts/build_hosts.py`, for example a table of frontmatter keys and values that the render inserts into every rendered `agents/*.md` frontmatter. Antigravity declares `enable_write_tools = true`, and Claude Code and Codex declare it present and empty, as the schema requires every key to be. The build gains the insertion step after slot filling and stripping, plus coverage in `tests/test_build_rendering.py`. The key exists only in Antigravity's own definition data, so `core/` names no host mechanism, the Claude Code and Codex trees never see it, and a future host gets the grant only by opting in. The `color` exception stays the only one. It adds new build code and a second frontmatter-rewriting mechanism next to stripping, and it has to settle several rules a one-key need does not obviously justify: agents only or skills too, how a TOML value is serialized into YAML (a boolean `true`, not the string), and ordering against a key core already carries. The insertion also has to be tested in-process, and that test runs only under the pinned interpreter.

Put a named slot placeholder (for example `{{AGENT_FRONTMATTER_EXTRA}}`) inside the frontmatter of both `core/agents/*.md` files. Antigravity's value file under `scripts/hosts/antigravity/slots/` holds `enable_write_tools: true`, and Claude Code and Codex declare the slot with an empty value file. The placeholder sits so that the value carries its own line ending, which means an empty value leaves no blank frontmatter line. No build code or setting changes. The existing `slot-declaration` and `unfilled-placeholder` checks keep the three definitions in step. It follows the recorded convention that whatever differs between hosts reaches `core/` only as a named slot every definition declares. The key appears only in the Antigravity tree, and nothing changes in `scripts/build_hosts.py` or its schema. Every slot so far carries prose wording. This one would carry a structural YAML key, and its correctness depends on newline placement inside frontmatter that no check validates beyond `yaml.safe_load` of the result. The core agent files also stop being readable as plain frontmatter, and two of the three hosts carry an empty value file that exists only to satisfy the declaration rule.

Write `enable_write_tools: true` into the frontmatter of both `core/agents/*.md` files and leave every host's `strip_frontmatter_keys` as it is, so the key renders into the Claude Code, Codex, and Antigravity trees alike as one each host is expected to ignore. Neither the build nor the settings change. It is the smallest change: two frontmatter lines and a rebuild, with no settings, slot, or build code to touch, and no way for the key to go missing from one tree through a definition edit. The Claude Code and Codex trees would name Antigravity's mechanism, which breaks the recorded development rule that a rendered tree never names another host's mechanism. No check enforces that rule, so only review would catch it. Whether Claude Code's agent loader and plugin validation silently accept an unknown frontmatter key is unverified. In Codex, the file is one the generic subagent is told to read and follow, so the key there is text the runner may take as an instruction about its tools.

open-question.question: Does scripts/build_hosts.py gain a check that fails --check when a rendered Antigravity agent file lacks enable_write_tools: true, so a later edit that drops the key is caught by the drift gate and CI, or is the on-demand agy suite the only guard against the key going missing?
open-question.alternative: scripts/build_hosts.py gains no check and no test is added: the build's check set stays as it is (dangling-plugin-root, foreign-plugin-root, stripped-key-present, frontmatter-missing/invalid/keys, unfilled-placeholder), and the on-demand agy suite's subagent write/shell probe is the only mechanical guard against a rendered Antigravity agent file losing enable_write_tools: true, with code review as the everyday guard. Adds nothing to the build, its settings key set, or the default pytest and CI runs. The guard sits on the observable behaviour (the agent actually writing and running commands), not on a key name, so it also catches the host renaming or reinterpreting the key, which no static check can. The suite runs only on request or when the integration changes, never in CI, so an edit that drops the key (a frontmatter cleanup in core/agents, a strip-list or setting change) passes --check and CI green and ships unnoticed until someone runs agy. That is the exact failure this milestone fixes, where all 11 dispatched subagents ended FAILED:. How easily the key can go missing depends on the sibling Write-tools key mechanism question.

Every host definition gains one new settings key, kept in the shared key set and left empty where a host has nothing to declare, naming the frontmatter keys and values each rendered agent file must carry (Antigravity: enable_write_tools = true; Claude Code and Codex: empty). check_host_tree gains a generic check, for example required-key-missing, that fails --check, and so the drift gate and CI, when a rendered agent lacks a declared key or carries a different value. The agy suite stays as the behavioural check beside it. A dropped key fails the drift gate and CI the moment it is committed, at no runtime cost. The check is host-neutral data plus generic Python, so it keeps the rule that adding a host means adding a definition directory with no host-specific Python, mirrors the existing stripped-key-present check, and serves any later host whose agents need a key. Adds a settings key every definition must declare and one more check to build_hosts.py and its documentation, for what is today a single key on one host. It checks the key only by name and value, so a host-side rename or change in meaning still reaches only the agy suite. If the sibling Write-tools key mechanism question settles on a per-host setting that inserts the key at render time, this check partly re-asserts the build's own output.

scripts/build_hosts.py gains a check written for this one case: when rendering the Antigravity tree, it fails --check, and so the drift gate and CI, if either rendered agent file's frontmatter lacks enable_write_tools: true. The host name and the key are written in the Python, and no settings key is added. The agy suite stays beside it. The smallest change that still puts the guard in --check and CI. One conditional and no new settings key or schema entry for the other definitions to declare. Puts host-specific Python into a build whose recorded rule is that no host-specific Python exists and adding a host means only adding a definition directory. It sets a precedent for per-host special cases in the generic gate and does nothing for a later host with the same need.

The build is unchanged. A test module under tests/ reads the committed hosts/antigravity/agents/*.md frontmatter and fails unless each file carries enable_write_tools: true. It runs in both default pytest runs, so CI catches a dropped key, since --check already forces the committed tree to match a fresh build. The agy suite stays beside it. Catches a dropped key in every CI run with no change to build_hosts.py, its check set, or any host definition's settings key set, so the build stays generic. Puts a host-tree assertion into a suite that otherwise tests the tools under core/tools, and hardcodes the host and key in a test instead of the definition's data. It also fails in pytest rather than in --check, so a maintainer running only the build loop finds out later, and it has to parse frontmatter without PyYAML to keep working at the 3.9 floor.

open-question.question: What do the installation docs say to a user whose project still holds a .agents/plugins/cairn/ copy extracted under an earlier release, which the host would discover beside the global copy — an instruction to remove it, a statement that a workspace-local copy is unsupported, or nothing?
open-question.alternative: The README's Antigravity installation section (the template under scripts/hosts/antigravity/ and the root README.md that carries it word for word) gains a short note for projects that extracted cairn under an earlier release: remove the project's .agents/plugins/cairn/ directory, with the literal command to do so and one clause on why (the old copy is discovered beside the global one, and it predates the subagents' write and shell tools). The note says nothing about how the host ranks or merges the two copies. Gives the one concrete action that removes the risk. A stale 1.8.5-or-earlier copy carries the agent files without enable_write_tools, so if the host loads it the user hits exactly the reported failure again. A command they can paste closes that off without needing to know how the host chooses between duplicates. Puts a destructive command in the install docs that every new reader sees, even though it only applies to projects that installed before this release. It also tells users to act on behaviour nobody has checked: how agy handles two plugins both named cairn, one global and one in .agents/plugins/, was not part of any hands-on check.

The README's Antigravity installation section states that the global ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn copy is the only supported installation and that a workspace-local .agents/plugins/cairn/ copy is unsupported. It gives no command and no removal instruction, and says nothing about how the host treats the two copies together. Draws the support line in one declarative sentence that stays true however agy ranks duplicate plugins. Bug reports from a project that still holds an old copy can be pointed back at that sentence, and the docs gain no destructive command. Leaves the user to work out that "unsupported" means "delete it", and that the old copy may be why subagents fail. Someone who skims past it can keep running a copy without write tools, see the reported FAILED: subagents, and get no hint of the cause.

This milestone first checks by hand what agy 1.4.0 does when a workspace holds a .agents/plugins/cairn/ copy beside the global one: whether it loads both, prefers one, or reports a conflict through agy plugin list. The README's Antigravity section then states the observed result and the action that follows from it, which is a removal instruction if the workspace copy is loaded or shadows the global one, and no note if the host ignores it. Bases the docs on what the host actually does rather than on an assumed conflict. The note is written only when it is needed, and when it is, it can say exactly what the user will see, so it holds no guess about precedence and no warning against a problem that doesn't exist. Adds one more hands-on probe to the milestone and makes the README wording depend on its outcome, so the docs task can't be written until the probe has run. The observed behaviour is pinned to one agy version and can drift on a later release without the note being rechecked.

The README's installation section describes only the fresh global install and says nothing about earlier copies. The advice to remove a project's .agents/plugins/cairn/ copy goes into the CHANGELOG.md entry for the release that moves the path, which /release-plugin writes at release time, so it reaches the people who are upgrading. Puts the migration advice where upgrading users look and keeps the install section clean for the far larger set of new readers. Once the release is old, the advice sits in history instead of lingering as a permanent caveat in the README. The milestone itself writes nothing, so whether the advice lands depends on the release step picking it up from the milestone's commits. A user who reinstalls from the README months later without reading the changelog never sees it.

The installation docs say nothing about workspace-local copies, now or later. The Antigravity section shows only the global extract command, and a project that still holds a .agents/plugins/cairn/ copy is left as it is. Keeps the docs to the one install path and adds no wording that depends on unverified host behaviour. The Antigravity tree has had few installs, so few projects, perhaps only the maintainer's own, are likely to hold an old copy at all. Any project that does hold an old copy is left exposed to the exact failure this milestone fixes: the host may load the stale agents, which lack enable_write_tools, and nothing in the docs points to the leftover directory as the cause.

open-question.question: Does the README's Antigravity installation section, now extracting into ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn once per machine rather than once per project, tell the user that the host discovers a new plugin directory only on startup and that a running agy session must be restarted after the extract, or does it keep to the extract command alone?
open-question.alternative: The Antigravity installation section in both the README template (scripts/hosts/antigravity/README.md) and the root README.md gets only the new global target: a mkdir -p and the curl | tar extract into ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn, with the template's existing paragraph on pinning a release by tag kept. Nothing is said about startup discovery or restarting a running agy session, for a first install or for an update. The section stays parallel to the Claude Code and Codex sections, which carry no restart or reload note, and the README states nothing about host behaviour beyond what the extract does, so there is no sentence to go stale if a later agy release starts discovering plugins while running. The CLI's own plugin guide says a new plugin directory is discovered only on startup, so a user who extracts while an agy session is open finds no /cairn: skills there and has no hint why. The move to a once-per-machine install makes that more likely, since the user is now installing outside any one project's session.

Both the README template and the root README.md follow the extract command with one sentence: Antigravity discovers a new plugin directory only on startup, so restart any agy session that was running during the extract. The note covers the first install only and says nothing about re-extracting a newer release over an existing global copy. It states exactly what agy's built-in plugin guide documents, a new directory found only on startup, and nothing more. One sentence heads off the likeliest first-run failure (cairn missing from the session that is already open) without claiming any unverified behaviour. It says nothing about updates. Whether skills changed by re-extracting over an existing ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn take effect in a running session is not documented or verified, so a user updating mid-session may still run stale skill text. It also adds a host-behaviour claim to the README that has to be kept true if agy changes.

Both the README template and the root README.md follow the extract command with a note covering every extract: restart any running agy session after installing, and again after re-extracting a newer or pinned release over the global copy, because the host reads the plugin's directory and skills at startup. One rule covers both the first install and every update, including the tag-pinning path the template already describes. A user never runs a session that mixes the old skill text with the new tool files. The update half goes beyond what the host documents, which is that a new directory is discovered only on startup. Unless this milestone's hands-on check confirms it, the README asserts reload behaviour nobody has verified, and the restart it asks for after an update may be unnecessary.

Both the README template and the root README.md follow the extract command with the first-install restart sentence (a new plugin directory is discovered only on startup, so restart a running agy session) plus a verification command, agy plugin list, which should show cairn enabled at ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn. Updates are not addressed. The user can confirm that the global copy landed where the host looks, which is the exact failure the milestone fixes, the orchestrator not finding the plugin at the path it expected. And the restart sentence covers the one case where the copy is in place but the open session cannot see it. It adds a second command and ties the README to the agy plugin list output and its subcommand name, which no other host's section does and which a CLI change can make wrong. A listing shows the plugin is installed, not that the running session has loaded it, so the restart sentence is still what fixes the open-session case.

alternative.id: Restart note in host README only

open-question.alternative: The first-install restart sentence follows the extract command only in the README template, which renders into the cairn-antigravity distribution repository's landing page. The root README.md's Antigravity section keeps to the extract command into ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn alone. The root README stays a terse install index whose host sections all have the same shape, and the host-specific detail lives on the page an Antigravity user lands on when installing from that host's distribution repository. The two sections, which today carry the same install command, drift apart, and a user who installs from the root README, the project's main landing page, never sees the note. Keeping two copies of one section in lockstep becomes a judgment call rather than a copy.

open-question.question: Does the milestone correct the sentence in docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md stating that an agy run loads the plugin from its working directory, which the global install makes false, or is the documentation change limited to the README's Antigravity installation section and the host definition's own comments?
open-question.alternative: The documentation change stays limited to the Antigravity installation section of the root README.md and of the scripts/hosts/antigravity/README.md template, plus the host definition's own comments; the docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md sentence saying an agy run loads the plugin from its working directory is left as it stands, and so is every other tracked mention of the workspace-local path (the bug issue template's manifest location, the distribution README's opening sentence about extraction into a workspace's .agents/plugins/cairn/). Keeps the milestone's documentation diff to the two installation sections the goal names, with nothing outside the install path and host definition to review or keep in step. Ships a release whose own docs contradict it: the headless-chain page tells an agy user the plugin is loaded from the project's working directory, and the bug template and distribution README intro point at a .agents/plugins/cairn path the global install no longer uses, so a user following them looks in the wrong place.

Beyond the two installation sections and the host definition's comments, the milestone rewrites the --add-dir bullet in docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md so it no longer says an agy run loads the plugin from its working directory: the run still takes its working directory as its workspace and works on the project there, while the plugin comes from the global install. Other tracked mentions of the workspace-local path (the bug issue template's manifest location, the distribution README's opening sentence) are left unchanged. Corrects the one statement outside the installation sections that describes how an agy run behaves at runtime, the one a headless-chain user acts on, with a one-sentence edit and no wider sweep. Leaves two other stale references in place: the bug report form still asks Antigravity users for the version at .agents/plugins/cairn/plugin.json, and the published distribution README still says its tree is laid out for extraction into a workspace's .agents/plugins/cairn/, both of which name a path a globally installed user does not have.

The milestone corrects every tracked, non-historical statement that names the workspace-local plugin path or says the plugin loads from the working directory: the two installation sections and the host definition's comments, the --add-dir bullet in docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md, the Antigravity manifest location in .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug.yml (to ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn/plugin.json), and the opening sentence of the scripts/hosts/antigravity/README.md template that describes extraction into a workspace's .agents/plugins/cairn/. CHANGELOG.md entries and finished milestones' files stay as written, being records of past releases. Leaves no tracked surface a user reads — headless-chain guide, bug form, distribution landing page — naming a path the release no longer installs to, so the global location is the one place every document points. Widens the milestone's documentation diff to files outside the installation sections, including the issue template and the distribution README intro, each of which must be reworded and reviewed; what the reworded text says about a leftover workspace-local copy depends on the sibling question on stale workspace-local copies.

open-question.question: Where does the on-demand agy suite live and how is it kept out of uv run pytest and the CI job — a marked module under tests/ that a default addopts deselects and an explicit marker selects, a directory outside pytest's testpaths that is run by naming its path, or a standalone script outside pytest invoked directly — given that the default run must stay unchanged on a machine with no agy?
open-question.alternative: The suite is a pytest module under tests/ (for example tests/test_agy.py) whose tests carry an agy marker. pyproject.toml's [tool.pytest.ini_options] registers the marker and gains addopts = -m "not agy", so uv run pytest and the 3.9 floor run (which reads the same pyproject.toml config) deselect it. It is invoked as uv run pytest -m agy, whose -m overrides the addopts one. It is the standard pytest idiom for opt-in tests. The suite lives in the one tests/ directory beside the existing modules, keeps the flat test_<name>.py naming, and reuses tests/conftest.py's REPO_ROOT, tool paths, and fixtures directly. The default runs do not stay fully unchanged. pyproject.toml's pytest config gains its first addopts and marker, both default runs (CI included) still import and collect the module and report it as deselected, so the module must import cleanly under 3.9 on a machine with no agy. And any later -m expression a contributor passes replaces the deselection and can pull the agy tests in.

The suite is a pytest module under tests/ whose file name falls outside pytest's default test_*.py collection pattern (for example tests/agy_suite.py). With testpaths = ["tests"] unchanged and no addopts, uv run pytest never collects it, while pytest collects any file named explicitly on its command line whatever its name. It is invoked by naming its path: uv run pytest tests/agy_suite.py. Nothing changes in pyproject.toml, the CI workflow, or what either default run imports or reports, so a machine with no agy sees exactly today's run. The module still shares tests/conftest.py and its fixtures. The exclusion rests only on an unstated naming convention. A later rename to the test_ prefix, or a python_files change, silently puts agy-driving tests into CI and the default run with nothing to catch it. It also breaks the repository's recorded "one flat test_<name>.py per concern" layout for tests/.

The suite is a pytest module under tests/ (for example tests/test_agy.py), and tests/conftest.py adds it to collect_ignore unless an opt-in environment variable (for example CAIRN_AGY=1) is set. Unset, the module is not collected, so neither default run imports or reports it. pyproject.toml is unchanged. It is invoked as CAIRN_AGY=1 uv run pytest tests/test_agy.py, or with the bare uv run pytest under the variable. The exclusion is an explicit, coded switch that a rename cannot defeat, and the default runs neither collect nor mention the module. The suite keeps the flat test_ naming, the shared conftest fixtures, and pyproject.toml's config untouched. It adds a conditional collection rule and a new environment-variable name to tests/conftest.py, which until now holds only fixtures. Invoking the suite means remembering a variable rather than a pytest option or a path. And a variable left exported in a maintainer's shell quietly turns every later default run into a slow agy run.

The suite is a pytest directory outside testpaths (for example agy_tests/ at the repository root), with its own conftest.py. testpaths = ["tests"] and the CI workflow stay as they are, so uv run pytest and the floor run never reach it. It is invoked by naming the directory: uv run pytest agy_tests. Where the suite sits says that it is excluded, so no config line, file-name convention, or environment variable has to hold. Both default runs are byte-for-byte unchanged, and the suite can grow its own fixtures (temporary workspaces, agy invocation helpers) without touching the tool suite's conftest. It adds a new top-level directory to the recorded repository layout and cannot use tests/conftest.py's fixtures without importing across directories or duplicating them. A contributor running pytest on the whole repository (uv run pytest .) would collect it.

The suite is a self-contained Python script outside pytest entirely (for example scripts/agy_suite.py beside build_hosts.py and set_version.py), invoked directly as uv run scripts/agy_suite.py or python3 scripts/agy_suite.py. It drives each agy -p process, checks its own pass conditions, prints its own per-check report, and signals the outcome through its exit status. No pytest file, marker, config line, or collection rule is involved. No pytest configuration or discovery path can ever reach the suite, so the default runs and CI are untouched by construction. It sits with the other maintainer-invoked scripts that are run by name, and a prerequisite check can stop the whole run cleanly before any agy process starts. It gives up pytest's assertion reporting, tmp_path and fixtures, and per-test selection, so the script must hand-roll its own checks, temporary workspaces, and summary. It also puts a test harness into a directory that today holds only build and release tooling. How it handles a missing agy is owned by the sibling question on running without agy, which this option's shape constrains to a whole-run stop or a hand-written skip.

open-question.question: Which plugin copy does the agy suite drive — the copy already installed at ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn as it stands, the freshly built hosts/antigravity/ tree that the suite installs over that path before running, or a copy installed under an isolated HOME the suite sets for the agy process so the user's own installation is never touched?
open-question.alternative: Source: the copy already at ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn, whatever release or build it holds. Location: the user's real HOME. Install step: none. The suite installs, compares, and restores nothing. It drives agy against that path and leaves keeping the copy current to the person running it. It is the simplest suite and never writes outside its fixture workspace. It exercises exactly the installation a user has, the same path the kinga_page failure ran against, and it can never disturb the user's own setup. A pass or fail says nothing about the change under test unless the user remembered to re-extract the freshly built tree first. Today the copy is a byte-identical 1.8.5 tree carrying the old .agents/plugins/cairn literal and no enable_write_tools key, so a run made after the milestone's build changes, with no reinstall, would test the old tree and report its old failures, or a stale pass.

Source: the copy already at ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn. Location: the user's real HOME. Install step: none, but before any agy process starts the suite compares that copy byte for byte with the repository's hosts/antigravity/ tree and stops on any difference, naming the remedy (re-extract or copy the built tree). It writes nothing to the user's installation. Every run is guaranteed to test the current build while the suite still never writes to the user's installation. Replacing the copy stays an explicit act of the user's own, and a stale install is caught rather than silently tested. Every build change makes the developer copy the tree by hand before the suite will run, which turns a one-command check into two steps. The comparison has to define which files count (the tree's README, .github workflow, and LICENSE ship too). How the suite reports a missing copy, as opposed to a different one, belongs to the sibling question on running without agy.

Source: the freshly built hosts/antigravity/ tree. Location: the user's real HOME. Install step: before running, the suite replaces ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn with a copy of the built tree and leaves it there afterwards, with no backup or restore. One command always tests the current build, at the exact global path the milestone standardizes on, with the user's real agy credentials, trusted folders, and git identity. The resulting install is also the next release's tree, so the maintainer's own agy setup tracks the build. The suite silently overwrites the user's own installation with an unreleased build. Every other project the user runs agy in (kinga_page, for one) then loads that development tree until the user re-extracts a release, and a running agy session picks it up only on restart. A run on a contributor's machine replaces their installed release without asking.

Source: the freshly built hosts/antigravity/ tree. Location: the user's real HOME. Install step: the suite moves any existing ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn aside, copies the built tree into that path, runs, and on exit (pass, fail, or interrupt) removes its copy and moves the user's original back. If no copy stood there before, it leaves none behind. It tests the current build at the real global path with the user's real credentials and environment, and it leaves the user's installation as it found it once the run ends. While the suite runs, every agy session on the machine sees the development tree. A crash or kill between the move and the restore can strand the original under a backup name and leave the development tree installed. The suite also needs delete and move logic over a directory inside the user's own configuration, which is the riskiest code it would carry.

Source: the repository's hosts/antigravity/ tree itself, not a copy. Location: the user's real HOME. Install step: ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn is made a symbolic link to the checkout's hosts/antigravity/ (once by the developer, or by the suite whenever the path is not already that link) and stays in place, so every rebuild is live at the global path with no install step per run. The suite always drives the current build, and no copying happens on any run. The maintainer's agy picks up each rebuild the way their Claude Code setup already loads hosts/claude live. Whether agy resolves the link and reports the skill's absolute SKILL.md path as the repository location rather than ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn has not been verified. A suite meant to prove global plugin-root resolution could therefore pass against a path no user install ever has. Every agy session on the machine also loads uncommitted development state, and a user who installs releases is left with a link instead.

Source: the freshly built hosts/antigravity/ tree. Location: a temporary directory the suite creates and sets as HOME for each agy process. Install step: the suite copies the built tree to that directory's .gemini/config/plugins/cairn, and copies in the minimum agy needs to run (the OAuth credentials and account files under ~/.gemini, plus a git identity for the fixture's commits). It never writes to the user's real ~/.gemini. Every run tests the current build at the global path's real shape, relative to the HOME the process sees, and it never touches the user's installation or any running agy session. Leftover state from an earlier run or a stale workspace-local copy cannot leak in. Whether agy 1.4.0 derives its config root from HOME, and authenticates from copied oauth_creds.json alone without a keychain or a fresh login, is unverified. The suite would also copy live OAuth credentials into a temp directory. Changing HOME changes git config, uv caches, and anything else the run reads from it. Whether the tree's plugin-root literal resolves inside the isolated HOME depends on the sibling question on the plugin-root literal form.

open-question.question: How does the agy suite exercise a subagent's write and shell tools and what signal does it accept as a pass — a full /cairn:provide-alternatives-to-all-open-questions run on a fixture milestone, passing when the alternatives land in open_questions.xml and its commit, or a minimal headless prompt that dispatches the agent directly with a trivial write-and-run task, passing on the agent's final message or a file it lands?

Which surfaces does the suite's plugin-root resolution test cover — the orchestrator's file read of a shared procedure, its python3 tool command, and the same two inside a dispatched agent, or only the tool command — given that the report's failures showed up on both the file read and the command?
open-question.alternative: The resolution test covers all four surfaces in both rendered agents: the orchestrator's file read of a shared procedure and its python3 tool command, and inside each dispatched agent (provide-alternatives-to-open-question and complete-task) its own file read of a shared procedure (alternatives-procedure.md, complete-procedure.md) and its own tool command (open_questions.py, task_list.py), each surface asserted separately. Every place the report saw a path fail is pinned, and each agent's distinct procedure file and tool is exercised, so a literal form that resolves in the shell but not in the host's file-reading tool, or in the orchestrator but not in an agent whose prompt carries no plugin path, fails a named assertion rather than a later run. It is the costliest shape: at least two agent dispatches per run, each a slow headless agy process using model calls, and complete-task needs a fixture task it can complete; how cheaply the agent surfaces can be reached depends on the shape the subagent probe takes and the fixture workspace the suite uses.

The resolution test covers all four surfaces — the orchestrator's file read of a shared procedure and its python3 tool command, and the same two inside one dispatched agent (provide-alternatives-to-open-question, the agent the report observed failing) — and does not dispatch complete-task for resolution. Both failure surfaces are covered in both contexts the report distinguishes, including the agent whose prompt carries no plugin path, at the cost of a single agent dispatch; both agents' rendered literals come from the same plugin_root, so one agent stands in for the other's resolution. complete-task's own read of complete-procedure.md and its task_list.py command go unexercised, so a fault specific to that agent file's rendering or context is caught only by its write-tools probe, if that probe touches those paths; whether it does depends on the shape the subagent probe takes.

The resolution test covers the orchestrator only, on both surfaces: its file read of a shared procedure and its python3 tool command; no dispatched agent's resolution is asserted by this test. It pins both failure modes the report observed in the orchestrator — the view_file stat failure and python's exit 2 — in one headless agy process with no dispatch, keeping the test fast and its pass signal simple. The dispatched agent, whose prompt carries no plugin path and which never sees the absolute SKILL.md path the orchestrator receives, is exactly where a form that relies on that metadata would fail, and this test does not look there; agent-side resolution is then verified only if the subagent probe happens to exercise it, which depends on the shape that probe takes.

The resolution test covers the python3 tool command only, in both contexts: once run by the orchestrator and once run inside a dispatched agent; no file read of a shared procedure is asserted in either. A failed command is loud and mechanically checkable (a non-zero exit and a no-such-file line in the transcript or output), whereas a failed file read may be silently recovered by the model searching for the file, so the test keys on the unambiguous signal while still covering the agent context the orchestrator's metadata does not reach. The host's file-reading tool and the shell resolve paths differently (the shell expands a tilde or $HOME, a file-reading tool may not), so a literal form that passes the command check can still break every shared-procedure read; whether that gap matters depends on the literal form chosen for the plugin root.

The resolution test covers one surface in one context: the orchestrator's python3 tool command; neither file reads nor any dispatched agent is asserted. It is the smallest, fastest, and least flaky test: one headless agy process, no dispatch, and a pass signal (the tool's output or exit status) that needs no transcript inspection. It covers one of the four places the report's failures appeared, leaving the file-read surface and the agent context — the two places a literal form is most likely to resolve differently — to be caught only by a later real run; how much that leaves exposed depends on the literal form chosen for the plugin root.

The suite carries no separate resolution test: plugin-root resolution is treated as verified whenever the end-to-end subagent check passes, since that run cannot succeed unless the orchestrator's and the agent's reads and commands resolved; no surface is asserted on its own. It adds no extra agy process or assertion beyond what the suite already runs, keeping the on-demand suite as short and cheap as possible while still failing when resolution is broken. A failure reports only that the run failed, not which surface or context broke, and a model that recovers from a failed read by searching for the file can pass with a broken literal; whether the end-to-end check touches any given surface at all depends on the shape the subagent probe takes.

open-question.question: In what workspace does the agy suite run each headless agy process — a temporary git repository the suite seeds through the plugin's own tools with a milestone and open questions, a committed fixture directory under tests/fixtures/ copied to a temporary location, or the cairn repository checkout itself?

Does the agy suite pin the model, effort, and print timeout it passes on each agy -p line, or run at the host's defaults with no --model, --effort, or --print-timeout as the headless chains in docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md do?

When the agy suite is invoked on a machine where agy is not on PATH or the global plugin copy it needs is absent, does it skip its tests, fail them, or stop before any test with one line naming the missing prerequisite?
open-question.alternative: Before any test runs, the suite checks both prerequisites (agy resolvable on PATH, the global plugin copy present at ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn) in one up-front check. When either is missing, it stops the whole run with a non-zero exit and one line naming the missing prerequisite. It reports no per-test outcome, and it treats both prerequisites the same way. An explicitly requested verification can never come back green on a machine that verified nothing. The single line names the exact cause, and no agy process is started only to fail, which keeps the report readable for the contributor or release pre-flight that asked for the run. Aborting the run is only harmless if the suite is never collected as part of a broader run. If it lives somewhere a wholesale pytest invocation reaches it (the Suite location and invocation axis), a session-level stop on a machine without agy breaks that unrelated run instead of passing it by. It also needs a session-level hook or a separate entry point rather than the ordinary per-test idiom.

Every suite test is skipped with a reason naming the missing prerequisite, and the run exits 0. This is a module-level skip in the manner of tests/test_build_rendering.py, which skips itself below Python 3.11 keyed on a condition checked before anything else, or one equivalent message and a zero exit if the suite is not pytest. Both prerequisites are treated the same way. It follows the repository's one existing conditional-module convention and the standard pytest idiom. That makes it harmless wherever the suite is collected on a machine without agy, CI's ubuntu job included, so the default run stays unchanged whatever the suite's location turns out to be. A run someone asked for on a misconfigured machine exits 0 with everything skipped, and the exit code reads as success. A contributor gate or release pre-flight that keys on the result can then pass without exercising agy at all, which defeats the point of a suite that runs only when someone wants the integration verified.

The suite is collected and run as normal, and each test (through a shared fixture or per-test guard) fails with a message naming the missing prerequisite. The run exits non-zero and reports one failure per test, and both prerequisites are treated the same way. It stays within ordinary per-test pytest machinery, needing no session-level abort hook, while still guaranteeing that a requested run on an unprepared machine cannot read as a pass. The report shows as many identical failures as the suite has tests, which buries the single real cause. It shares the stop option's hazard of turning any broader collection on a machine without agy red (the Suite location and invocation axis), with noisier output.

The two prerequisites are treated differently. When agy is not on PATH, every test is skipped with a reason naming agy and the run exits 0, because the machine simply cannot run the suite. When agy is present but the global plugin copy is absent, the run fails non-zero with a line naming the missing copy, because the installation this milestone standardizes on is missing on a machine set up for agy. The outcome follows what the absence means. A machine without the host is not a finding, while a host without the global install is exactly the kind of setup fault the global-path standardization is meant to rule out, so it is reported loudly. The split only makes sense if the suite drives the pre-installed global copy. If it installs its own copy, the second prerequisite never arises (the Suite plugin copy axis). It also keeps the skip option's risk that a requested run on a machine without agy exits 0, and it is two rules to document instead of one.

The suite skips with a reason naming the missing prerequisite and exits 0 by default. An explicit switch the suite documents (an environment variable or command-line flag) turns the same missing prerequisite into a stop before any test, with a non-zero exit and one line naming it. Both prerequisites get the same treatment in each mode. Any accidental or wholesale collection stays harmless, and a deliberate verification (a contributor gate or release pre-flight) can still demand that a missing prerequisite fail instead of passing silently. It adds a second mode and a switch that every invoking site must remember to set. A gate that forgets the flag silently falls back to the skip behaviour and its false green. It is also more mechanism than a suite that already runs only on request may need.

The suite adds no detection of either prerequisite. Its tests invoke agy and read the global copy directly, and on a machine lacking either they fail with whatever the subprocess or agy itself raises: a FileNotFoundError for a missing binary, or agy's own error or a failed resolution for a missing copy. It adds no code and leaves no prerequisite list to keep in step with what the tests actually use. Any missing piece still makes the run non-zero. The failure names no prerequisite. A missing global copy surfaces as a plugin-root resolution failure that looks exactly like the bug the suite exists to detect, so an unprepared machine produces a misleading regression report rather than a setup message.

open-question.question: How is the goal's rule that the agy suite runs when the Antigravity host integration changes realized, with CI ruled out — a CONTRIBUTING.md sentence naming the paths whose change requires a run before committing, a pre-flight step in the release-plugin skill, or both?

What becomes of the dated hands-on-check block in the header of scripts/hosts/antigravity/settings.toml once a repeatable suite exists — this milestone's run updates it to name agy 1.4.0, the global path, and the write-tools check and it stays the one record of what was checked, or it is replaced by a pointer to the suite as the way to re-check?
open-question.alternative: This milestone's hands-on run rewrites the dated block in the header of scripts/hosts/antigravity/settings.toml as a new check against agy 1.4.0. The block names the global ~/.gemini/config/plugins/cairn path as the install checked, the enable_write_tools check on both agents, and the points the 2026-10-13 run sourced (dispatch, waiting, continuing an agent, context file), each re-checked or carried forward. It stays the one record of what was checked. The block carries no reference to the agy suite, and the CLAUDE.md invariant stays as worded. Keeps the recorded invariant exactly as it stands: one dated block per host that a later re-check updates. Every slot value's provenance and the installed version checked stay in one committed place, with no CLAUDE.md edit. The suite and the block record overlapping facts (plugin-root resolution, write tools) with nothing linking them. A later suite run against a newer agy updates nothing in the block, so the block's version and date go stale without anything showing it, and a reader of the host definition is never told that a repeatable re-check exists.

This milestone's run rewrites the dated block as a new check against agy 1.4.0, naming the global path, the enable_write_tools check, and the carried or re-checked slot-sourcing points, and the block stays the one record of what was checked. One added line in the header names the agy suite as the way to re-check the points it covers. The CLAUDE.md invariant keeps its one-record rule and gains at most a clause allowing that pointer. Keeps one committed record with the version and date checked, and also tells the next editor of the host definition how to repeat the automatable part of the check rather than redoing it by hand. The pointer is a second kind of content in a header the invariant reserves for the check record. The block's points still duplicate what the suite asserts, so a suite run that passes against a newer agy still leaves the block naming 1.4.0 unless someone also updates the block by hand. How exactly the pointer names the suite depends on where the suite lives and how it is invoked (the Suite location and invocation question).

The block keeps only the points the suite does not exercise: the slot-sourcing facts about dispatch, waiting, continuing an agent, and the context file, dated to the run that last checked them. The points the suite covers (global plugin-root resolution, subagent write and shell tools) are recorded by the suite's own tests, not written into the block, and the header carries one line pointing at the suite for them. The CLAUDE.md invariant is reworded so that a host's check lives in its settings.toml block for points no suite covers and in the suite for points it does. Each fact has exactly one home, and the home matches how it is re-checked: the automatable points live in the suite and are re-verified whenever it runs, so they cannot drift from a stale prose copy, while the hand-checked slot provenance keeps its dated record. A host's check is split across two places, which reverses the "recorded in one place only" invariant and needs a CLAUDE.md change. Suite runs are not committed, so the installed agy version the suite last passed against is recorded nowhere, and the block's own date then covers only part of what the host was checked for.

The dated block is removed from the header of scripts/hosts/antigravity/settings.toml and replaced by a pointer naming the agy suite as the way to check the host. The suite's tests become the record of what is checked for Antigravity, and no dated version-and-points block remains for this host. The CLAUDE.md invariant is rewritten for Antigravity, or for any host with such a suite, to name the suite rather than a settings.toml block. Removes the hand-maintained prose record outright for this host. What is checked is whatever the suite asserts, re-verified on every run, so no dated block can say something the current host no longer does. The suite exercises plugin-root resolution and write and shell tools, not the dispatch, waiting, continuing, and context-file facts that sourced the eight slot values, so their provenance is lost unless the suite grows to cover them, which the goal does not ask for. The installed version checked leaves the committed record, since suite runs are not committed, and Antigravity's record then takes a different form from Codex's and Claude Code's.

The 2026-10-13 block against agy 1.3.4 is neither updated nor pointed at the suite: this milestone's checks go unrecorded in settings.toml, and the block stays a dated historical record of that earlier run. Changing it is left to a later milestone, or never done. At most, the clause tying it to "the plugin_root path below" is reworded so it no longer describes the new global path. No edit to the header and no CLAUDE.md change. A dated block that says what was checked on its date stays true as history, and the suite carries the new checks without any decision about how the two records relate. Goes against the invariant's own rule that a later re-check updates the block: this milestone's run is such a re-check, against a newer agy and a different install path, and it would leave no committed trace. The block would keep describing a workspace-relative install the milestone makes unsupported, misleading the next editor about which version and which layout the slot values were last confirmed against.
